newsitem.title: FINLAND: Nokia sees more handset fragmentation. [CORRECTED 12:25 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Nokia sees more handset fragmentation. [CORRECTED 12:25 GMT]

text.p: Marking the 10th anniversary of its first hand-portable phone for Finland, Europe's mobile phone major Nokia Oy is looking towards a global handset market which is increasingly fragmented.

"Look at the (phone's) physical format: it might not just be a block, it might be...integrated into your clothing," Anssi Vanjoki, Nokia's head of mobile phone sales for Europe, Africa and the Gulf states, said in a telephone interview on Friday.

Ten years ago this week Nokia launched the analogue Mobira Cityman, in its time a featherweight at 770 g (1.7 lb) and retailing in Finland at 24,000 markka ($5,000) a piece. In the product's life, Nokia sold a total of 9,000 units.

For Finland, which has since evolved into the world's most densely "mobile" country, that was a ground-breaking innovation: Nokia's first wireless launch in 1982 was a carphone weighing 11 kg (24 lb), or the rough equivalent of a crate of beer.
"In those days it was a very macho thing... always something to do with cars," said Vanjoki.

Nokia does not today reveal unit sales but its mobile phones retail in Finland at about one-tenth of their 1987 price, weigh about a quarter of the 1987 total, and in 1996 the division generated over 21 billion markka in net sales.

Looking to the future, Vanjoki sketched a market for a "personal mobile communicator" which allows different voice and data functions, depending on the environment you are in. Part of it might be in your spectacles, another in your favourite suit.

At one end of the market you might want to be able constantly to chat hands-free with your friends; at another you might want a large data display because your business demands that you spend a lot of time on the Internet.
Vanjoki said miniaturisation continues to be key in mobile markets, but data in wireless telephony is another major step.

This is an area where Nokia claims a lead: Vanjoki said its rivals have yet to compete seriously with the 9000 Communicator, which it launched as an industry first last year and combines voice, fax, Internet and e-mail options in a handset.
"What amazes us is that there is no competition," he said.

Nokia also recently presented to operators the concept of direct Internet access through a simple handset, and is planning a new version of its latest 8110 model to include Internet access through smart messaging (SMS).
"This year is a major milestone year," Vanjoki said. "Nokia has introduced SMS which brings the Internet into every portable. It looks very likely that this will become the new standard in GSM."

Business users are key in the early development of the wireless data market, as they were in the early years of the hand portable phone. As advertisements in Finnish media marking the 10th anniversary recall, "in the beginning was the Yuppie".

A key piece in the global business jigsaw is the United States -- currently a relatively undeveloped digital mobile market and where Code Division, Multiple Access (CDMA) has rivalled Europe's Global System for Mobile Communications (corrects name of standard from Groupe Speciale Mobile) (GSM) as a standard.

Nokia is on schedule to launch a CDMA phone this summer, Vanjoki said. He expects the data side of mobile telephony to take off in the United States around the turn of the century, and the country to become a world-leader.
"We intend to have a big share of that market in future," he added.
